new_statements.quote: Stress is phonemic, e.g. siká 'you, familiar' vs. síka 'dysentery'. There, are, however, certain environments that attract stress. Stress falls on the last syllable if the penultimate syllable is closed, i.e., the last vowel is preceded by two consonants (including a sequence of glottal stop + consonant): paltóg 'gun', takkí 'excrement', kulagtít 'jerking movement', tig-ʔáb 'belch', lisʔá 'nit, lice egg', pugtó 'guess'. Exceptions to this rule include words of foreign origin or words with a velar nasal coda preceding a final syllable: súngka 'kind of native game', bibíngka 'rice cake', karámba 'jar' (Spanish loan), kuárto 'room' (Spanish loan). Stress also falls on the last syllable if the last vowel is preceded by a consonant and glide: sadiá 'renowned', bituén 'star', aniá 'what'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (minimal pairs siká/síka), on the ultima or penult; it is predictably final when the penult is closed (two consonants, incl. glottal stop + C, before the last vowel) or when the last vowel follows consonant + glide; words with two identical CVC sequences separated by a vowel stress that vowel (salísal, batíbat); stressed open syllables and vowels before geminates are lengthened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Open reduplicated syllables in roots that contain a vowel sequence also bear secondary stress/lengthening: na.ka-bà-baín (POT-RDP-shame) shameful.'
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords and words with a velar-nasal coda before the final syllable escape the closed-penult rule (súngka, bibíngka, karámba, kuárto); loans aránia, hópia escape the consonant+glide rule; yakayák, pidipíd are exceptions to the CVC-V-CVC rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Peace Corps 1968 is based on speakers from Vigan (Ilocos Sur) and Laoag (Ilocos Norte) and notes La Union vs. northern dialect differences for the vowel /e/ only; Williams 1904 §6 lists dialectal pronunciation variants (sabuet/sabat/sebbat..) without dialect-specific accent differences; López/Carro and Swift describe the Ilocos standard of the Spanish-era grammars. No work describes a dialect-specific stress system. Vibo y Inderias 1920 is a grammar of Spanish written in Ilokano, not a description of Ilokano.

new_statements.quote: Accents are of two kinds, radical and accidental. The radical accent is the accent of the root, unaffected by prefixes, suffixes, or in general by inflection. Thus the accent of súrat or of quíta is on the penult. [...] (B). The accent is on the ultimate: [...] 5. Where the vowel of the ultimate is preceded by two consonants, as: aplág, appán, bontóc, bantót, etc. This rule is universal and applies also to words where the consecution of consonants is caused by conjugation or by inflection. [...] No complete rules can be laid down for accents. Many words that are identical in spelling will vary in meaning, as the accent may determine. Examples: árac (wine), arác (to gather for a festival); bágui (part or portion), baguí (body); basá (wetness), bása (to read); átob (a small aperture), otób (to consider); etc. It is evident that in this, as in other languages, the accent of many words can only be learned by study and observation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Root ('radical') accent is on the penult or the ultima and is partly lexical (minimal pairs); rules attributed to 'Narro' [sic, presumably Naves/Carro]: penult in words with identical vowels flanking (dáan), in reduplicated disyllables (patongpátong), in CVC-V-CVC words (bisíbis), etc; ultima in reduplicated closed monosyllables (bacbác), in ay/ao reduplications (baybáy), before a hyphen (cay-ó), and universally when two consonants precede the last vowel (aplág). 'Accidental' accent: suffixes -an/-en move the accent to the root's last syllable (quíta > quitáen); syncope under -an/-en or ca-/ma-/na-/maca- makes the word oxytone (bariques > baricsén); amá, iná, apó become paroxytone after the article ni.
new_statements.exceptions: riquetriquét, gotocgotóc against the reduplication rule; 'No complete rules can be laid down for accents'.

new_statements.translation: [p. xiv] As for Prosody, or the quantity of syllables, we can surely dispense with another book, because up to now neither I, who have now dealt with this language for more than twenty-eight years, nor any other minister past or present, has found a trace of any rule that could be given for it; it can only be left to the ear [...] [p. 313] 'Penúltima producta' is said of every term whose penultimate vowel is pronounced with emphasis on it and as if lengthening it [...] 'Penúltima correcta' is said of every term whose last vowel is long, being pronounced with force [...] [p. 314] 5. Every word that has two consonants before its last vowel, e.g. aplág, appán, bantót; this rule is universal, not only for roots but also for compounds [...] [p. 338] 8. As a general rule it should be held that every root lacking a (written) accent is paroxytone, the pronunciation falling on the penultimate syllable

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as Rubino/Swift (Swift's rules are a translation of these); adds the penult-default statement and the 17th-century 'no rule, only the ear' classification; catalog rule field is empty.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two accent types, 'penúltima producta' (penult stressed and lengthened) and 'penúltima correcta' (final stressed); no general rule can be given, the ear decides, but sub-rules hold: penult in words with two like vowels in the middle (dáan), in reduplicated compounds (pátong-pátong), in words ending in a repetition of the first syllable (buquíbuc), etc; ultima in reduplicated closed syllables (abáb, bacbác), in ay/ao reduplications (baybáy), in hyphenated words (cay-ó), and universally when two consonants precede the last vowel (aplág); the orthography's default (unmarked) is penult. Accidental accents: -en/-an move the accent to the next vowel (quíta > quitáen); syncope with ca-/ma-/na-/maca- or -en/-an makes words oxytone (bángag > mabangág, bariques > baricsén); amá, iná, apó become paroxytone after sí/ni.
new_statements.exceptions: riguet-riguét, gotóc-gotóc (acút-acút in the Ortografía) are oxytone against the reduplication rule; saplít, ablát keep their accent under -en/-an; 'ng' counts as a single consonant for the two-consonant rule.

No work describes a dialect-specific stress system. Vibo y Inderias 1920 is a grammar of Spanish written in Ilokano, not a description of Ilokano.

new_statements.quote: Stress. Stress is phonemic. Thus the position of the stress distinguishes /bankú/ 'bench' from /bánku/ 'bank'. Stressed vowels are usually longer than unstressed vowels and also higher in pitch. However, if two or more syllables follow a stress, the syllable immediately following the stress has a higher pitch than the stressed syllable. [...] 3. Primary stress, which most frequently occurs on the syllable before the final syllable, is not marked in that position. When it occurs elsewhere, it is written with an acute accent (´).

new_statements.quote: Der Akzent besteht in einer etwas schleppenden Aussprache der Tonsilbe. Aehnlich ist der Akzent in den meisten andern indonesischen Sprachen. Die Tonsilbe ist gewöhnlich die letzte oder die vorletzte. Manchmal dient der Akzent als Mittel gleichlautende Wörter von verschiedener Bedeutung zu unterscheiden. Folgende Regeln lassen sich feststellen: Auf der vorletzten Silbe liegt der Ton: 1. Bei zweisilbigen Wurzeln, die am Ende der ersten und am Anfang der zweiten Silbe denselben Vokal haben: dáan, báak, bóos; 2. bei geminierten zweisilbigen Wurzeln: patongpatong, endagendag. [...] Auf der letzten Silbe betont sind: 1. Wörter mit zwei gleichen konsonantisch auslautenden Silben: abab, bakbak, batbat; [...] 3. Wörter, die vor dem Vokal der Endsilbe zwei Konsonanten haben: aplay, appan, bantot.
new_statements.translation: The accent consists in a somewhat drawn-out pronunciation of the tonic syllable. The accent is similar in most other Indonesian languages. The tonic syllable is usually the last or the second-to-last. Sometimes the accent serves as a means of distinguishing homophonous words of different meaning. The following rules can be established: The stress lies on the penultimate syllable: 1. in disyllabic roots that have the same vowel at the end of the first and the beginning of the second syllable: dáan, báak, bóos; 2. in geminated (reduplicated) disyllabic roots: patongpatong, endagendag. [...] Stressed on the last syllable are: 1. words with two identical consonant-final syllables: abab, bakbak, batbat; [...] 3. words that have two consonants before the vowel of the final syllable: aplay, appan, bantot.
new_statements.citation: Williams, Harold Whitmore (1904). Grammatische Skizze der Ilocano-Sprache : mit Berücksichtigung ihrer Beziehungen zu den anderen Sprachen der Malayo-polynesischen Familie. Straub.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (realized as a drawn-out syllable) is on the ultima or the penult and can distinguish homophones; penult in roots with like flanking vowels, reduplicated disyllables and CVC-V-CVC words; ultima in reduplicated closed monosyllables, ay/ao reduplications and words with two consonants before the last vowel. sources.quote: Der Akzent besteht in einer etwas schleppenden Aussprache der Tonsilbe. Aehnlich ist der Akzent in den meisten andern indonesischen Sprachen. Die Tonsilbe ist gewöhnlich die letzte oder die vorletzte. Manchmal dient der Akzent als Mittel gleichlautende Wörter von verschiedener Bedeutung zu unterscheiden. Folgende Regeln lassen sich feststellen: Auf der vorletzten Silbe liegt der Ton: 1. Bei zweisilbigen Wurzeln, die am Ende der ersten und am Anfang der zweiten Silbe denselben Vokal haben: dáan, báak, bóos; 2. bei geminierten zweisilbigen Wurzeln: patongpatong, endagendag. [...] Auf der letzten Silbe betont sind: 1. Wörter mit zwei gleichen konsonantisch auslautenden Silben: abab, bakbak, batbat; [...] 3. Wörter, die vor dem Vokal der Endsilbe zwei Konsonanten haben: aplay, appan, bantot.

sources.quote: "Stress is phonemic, e.g. siká 'you, familiar' vs. síka 'dysentery'. There, are, however, certain environments that attract stress. Stress falls on the last syllable if the penultimate syllable is closed, i.e., the last vowel is preceded by two consonants (including a sequence of glottal stop + consonant): paltóg 'gun', takkí 'excrement' ... Exceptions to this rule include words of foreign origin or words with a velar nasal coda preceding a final syllable: súngka, bibíngka, karámba (Spanish loan), kuárto (Spanish loan). tone.quote: 2.7. Pitch and intonation. The pitch of a normal Ilokano sentence or utterance generally stays on one level with only slight rises over stressed syllables. At the end of a sentence or utterance, the pitch may rise sharply after which it is cut off abruptly, as in yes-or-no and echo questions; or it may be cut off abruptly, without any appreciable rise or fall, as in ordinary statements. Within a sentence at phrase or clause breaks, and in hesitations, the pitch may be held or suspended momentarily at the same level. We shall call these three kinds of pitch terminals the question intonation, the declarative intonation, and the suspensatory intonation, respectively.
